questions.question: What does a Python backend interview cover and why does it exist? It assesses your grasp of Python's data model, its idioms, and the web/Django/FastAPI ecosystem — the skills a Python shop needs before hiring you.
questions.title: Python Backend Interview Overview
questions.direct_answer: A Python backend interview evaluates your understanding of Python's data model (everything is an object, mutable vs immutable, the descriptor protocol), its idioms (duck typing, comprehensions, decorators, generators), and the web ecosystem (Django, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy), at the level the role demands. It exists because Python's dynamic, duck-typed, batteries-included nature shapes how production code is written, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized both the language's power and its pitfalls (GIL, mutability, late binding) before hiring you to write backend services in it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what a Python interview uniquely tests — the data model (mutable/immutable, descriptors), idioms (decorators, generators, comprehensions), and the GIL/async story — not just Python syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a Python interview as a generic backend interview with simpler syntax — missing the data model, the GIL, decorators/generators, and the Django/FastAPI ecosystem that the interview actually probes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame the Python interview as testing the data model (objects, mutable/immutable, descriptors), idioms (decorators, generators, comprehensions, context managers), and the ecosystem (Django/FastAPI/SQLAlchemy) — plus the GIL/async story.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: A Python backend interview evaluates your understanding of Python's data model, its idioms, and the web ecosystem at the level the role demands. It exists because Python's dynamic, duck-typed, batteries-included nature shapes how production code is written, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized both the language's power and its pitfalls — the GIL, mutability, late binding — before hiring you to write backend services. The interview typically spans the language core (the data model, built-ins, comprehensions, decorators, generators), concurrency (the GIL, asyncio, threading vs multiprocessing), the web ecosystem (Django, FastAPI, Flask, SQLAlchemy), testing (pytest, mocking), and production concerns.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas a Python interview tests: (1) the data model — everything is an object; mutable vs immutable types (list vs tuple, dict) and the bugs mutability causes; the descriptor protocol and how attributes become properties; (2) idioms — decorators (functions that wrap functions), generators (lazy evaluation with yield), comprehensions, context managers (with); (3) duck typing and protocols — 'if it quacks like a duck'; structural typing via typing.Protocol; (4) the GIL and concurrency — the Global Interpreter Lock means threads don't parallelize CPU work; use multiprocessing or asyncio (single-threaded, cooperative); (5) the web ecosystem — Django (batteries-included), FastAPI (async, type-hinted), SQLAlchemy; (6) testing — pytest, fixtures, mocking; (7) production — packaging, typing (mypy), observability.

sections.content: The central tension is Python's ease versus its sharp edges: Python is readable and fast to write, but its dynamic typing, mutability, and the GIL create pitfalls (late-binding closures, shared mutable defaults, CPU-bound threads that don't parallelize) that the interview probes. A second tension: duck typing is powerful but can produce runtime errors static typing catches; the rise of type hints (mypy, pydantic) is the ecosystem's answer, and interviewers check whether you use them. The third: the web-ecosystem choice (Django vs FastAPI) is itself a design decision — Django is batteries-included and synchronous-friendly; FastAPI is async-first and type-hint-driven — and the interview may ask you to justify one.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Python interview tests the data model (mutable/immutable, descriptors), idioms (decorators, generators, comprehensions, context managers), and the GIL/async story.
Everything is an object; mutable vs immutable types (list vs tuple) are a classic bug source — know which is which.
The GIL means CPU-bound threads don't parallelize; use multiprocessing for CPU work, asyncio/threading for I/O work.
Decorators, generators, and comprehensions are core idioms — a generator is lazy (yield), a list is eager.
Duck typing + type hints (typing.Protocol, mypy, pydantic) are the modern balance of flexibility and safety.
The web-ecosystem choice (Django batteries-included vs FastAPI async/type-hinted) is itself a design decision the interview may probe.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A Python backend interview evaluates your understanding of Python's data model, its idioms, and the web ecosystem at the level the role demands. It exists because Python's dynamic, duck-typed, batteries-included nature shapes how production code is written, and an interviewer must verify you've internalized both the power and the pitfalls — the GIL, mutability, late binding. The data model I anchor on is that everything is an object and the mutable-versus-immutable distinction, like list versus tuple, is a classic bug source. The idioms are decorators, which wrap functions and are used for auth, logging, and caching; generators, which are lazy with yield and memory-efficient for large datasets; and comprehensions and context managers. The concurrency story is the GIL — the Global Interpreter Lock means CPU-bound threads don't parallelize, so I use multiprocessing for CPU work and asyncio or threading for I/O. The web ecosystem is Django, which is batteries-included and synchronous-friendly, versus FastAPI, which is async-first and type-hint-driven, and that choice is itself a design decision the interview may ask me to justify. The honest tension is Python's ease versus its sharp edges — it's readable and fast to write, but the dynamic typing, mutability, and GIL create pitfalls, and the rise of type hints with mypy and pydantic is the ecosystem's answer.

questions.title: Django ORM vs Raw SQL
questions.question: When would you use Django ORM versus raw SQL, and what are the trade-offs?

sections.content: The interviewer is testing whether you understand the ORM abstraction and its real-world costs. They want to hear a nuanced answer — not 'ORM always' or 'raw SQL always', but the specific conditions where each wins.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ORM for 90% of operations** — `select_related`, `prefetch_related`, and `annotate` cover most query patterns with security and portability built in
- **N+1 is the ORM's biggest trap** — every ForeignKey access in a loop fires a separate query; always profile with `django-debug-toolbar`
- **Raw SQL for complex aggregations** — CTEs, window functions, and `INSERT...SELECT` don't map cleanly to ORM expressions
- **`RawSQL` and `Func` bridge both worlds** — mix database-specific features into ORM queries without going fully raw
- **Never concatenate user input** — always use parameterized queries with `%s` placeholders to prevent SQL injection

Django ORM is the right default. It gives you security (parameterized queries prevent SQL injection), portability (switch from PostgreSQL to SQLite in tests), and expressive Python code that matches the domain model. For 90% of CRUD operations and even complex queries using `select_related`, `prefetch_related`, and `annotate`, ORM performs well.

Raw SQL wins in three cases: first, highly complex aggregations where the generated SQL is inefficient or the query planner benefits from explicit hints. Second, bulk operations like INSERT ... SELECT or complex CTEs that don't map cleanly to ORM expressions. Third, database-specific features like PostgreSQL window functions or JSONB operations — though Django's `Func` and `RawSQL` let you mix these in without fully abandoning the ORM.

The key smell that says 'go raw': you're calling `.query` to debug generated SQL and it looks absurd — 12 JOINs for a simple report. At that point, a named raw query in a repository class is cleaner and testable.

- **Always profile before optimizing** — use `django-debug-toolbar` or log queries in middleware
- **N+1 is the #1 ORM trap** — every ForeignKey access in a loop needs `select_related`
- **`only()` and `defer()`** reduce column fetching when you don't need all fields
- **`values()` and `values_list()`** return dicts/tuples instead of model instances — faster for read-only operations
- **Never concatenate user input into raw SQL** — always use parameterized queries with `%s` placeholders

sections.title: A decorator, a generator, and the GIL — Python idioms
sections.content:
```text
# (1) DECORATOR: a function that wraps another. Common for auth, logging, caching.
import functools
def timed(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*a, **k):
        import time; t = time.perf_counter()
        r = fn(*a, **k)
        print(f"{fn.__name__}: {time.perf_counter()-t:.3f}s")
        return r
    return wrapper

@timed
def load(n): return sum(range(n))
#   @timed is sugar for: load = timed(load)

# (2) GENERATOR: lazy evaluation with yield — produces values one at a time.
def stream_lines(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:        # never loads the whole file into memory
            yield line.strip()
#   Memory-efficient for large datasets; the interviewer checks you know
#   generators vs a list (lazy vs eager).

# (3) GIL: threads do NOT parallelize CPU-bound Python.
#   CPU-bound  -> multiprocessing (separate interpreters, real parallelism).
#   I/O-bound  -> asyncio or threading (release the GIL on I/O).
```

questions.title: Django Middleware
questions.question: How does Django middleware work, and how would you write custom middleware for authentication or request logging?

sections.content: They want to see that you understand the request/response lifecycle in Django, can explain the onion model of middleware, and can write clean, production-quality middleware.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Onion model execution** — middleware runs top-down on request, bottom-up on response, each layer wrapping the next
- **`__init__` runs once at startup** — expensive setup belongs there, not in `__call__` which runs per request
- **Cross-cutting concerns only** — authentication, logging, CORS, and rate limiting are ideal middleware candidates
- **Short-circuiting skips inner layers** — returning early without calling `get_response` bypasses the view and all remaining middleware
- **Async middleware for async views** — use `async def __call__` to avoid blocking the event loop

Django middleware is a layer in the request/response processing pipeline. Every request passes through all middleware in order (top to bottom in `MIDDLEWARE` settings), and the response passes back through in reverse order. Think of it as an onion — each middleware wraps the view.

Middleware is the right place for cross-cutting concerns: authentication checks, request logging, rate limiting, CORS headers, response compression. Each middleware class implements `__call__`, receives the request, decides whether to pass it to the next layer via `get_response(request)`, and can modify both request and response.

For authentication: check the Authorization header, decode a JWT, attach `request.user`. For logging: record the incoming request URL and method, call the next layer, record the response status and duration. Both patterns follow the same structure — do something before, call `get_response`, do something after.

- **Order matters** — middleware runs top-down on request, bottom-up on response
- **`__init__` is called once** at startup — put expensive initialization there, not in `__call__`
- **Don't block in middleware** — async views need async middleware (`async def __call__`)
- **`process_exception` hook** — handle exceptions from views without try/except in `__call__`
- **Short-circuit carefully** — returning early from `__call__` without calling `get_response` bypasses the entire view and remaining middleware

questions.title: Django Signals
questions.question: What are Django signals and when should you use them — and when should you avoid them?

sections.content: Interviewers want to see you understand both the value of signals (decoupling) and their dark side (hidden coupling, debugging difficulty). Many engineers overuse signals — demonstrating restraint is a green flag.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Observer pattern for decoupling** — `post_save`, `pre_save`, and `post_delete` let components react without the sender knowing
- **Infrastructure, not business logic** — signals are for audit logs, cache invalidation, and denormalization, not payment processing
- **Register in `AppConfig.ready()`** — avoids import-order issues that cause silent handler failures
- **Signals are synchronous** — handlers run inline before the response returns; use Celery for slow side effects
- **`created` flag is essential** — `post_save` fires on both INSERT and UPDATE; almost always check this parameter

Django signals implement the observer pattern — they let decoupled components react to events like model saves without the sender knowing who's listening. The most common signals are `post_save`, `pre_save`, and `post_delete` on models.

Good use cases: sending a welcome email after user creation, invalidating a cache when a model changes, creating related records (like a UserProfile for every new User). These are genuinely cross-cutting concerns where signals avoid coupling your User model to email, cache, and profile logic.

Where signals hurt: anything synchronous and business-critical. If the signal handler fails, you won't know at the call site. If you need to send an order confirmation email synchronously and handle errors cleanly, a direct function call is safer and testable. Also — signals make code flow hard to trace. A senior engineer reading the `User.save()` path won't know five signal handlers fire without checking every app's `apps.py`.

- **Register in `AppConfig.ready()`** — not at module level, to avoid import order issues
- **`created` parameter in `post_save`** — `True` on INSERT, `False` on UPDATE. Almost always check this.
- **Signals are synchronous** — they execute inline, before the response returns. Use Celery for anything slow.
- **Avoid signals in tests** — use `@override_settings` or signal disconnection to keep tests deterministic
- **`send_robust()`** — catches exceptions in handlers so one broken handler doesn't silently stop others

questions.title: Django Caching
questions.question: How does Django's caching framework work, and what caching strategies would you use for a high-traffic API?

sections.content: They want to hear that you know the cache levels (per-view, per-fragment, per-object), can configure Redis as the backend, understand cache invalidation patterns, and have thought about cache stampedes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three cache levels** — `@cache_page` for full responses, `{% cache %}` for template fragments, `cache.get/set` for objects
- **Redis via `django-redis`** — production standard with `IGNORE_EXCEPTIONS: True` for graceful degradation
- **Version your cache keys** — bumping a version number invalidates all keys without flushing the entire cache
- **Stampede prevention** — use distributed locks or pre-warming to prevent thundering herd on cache expiry
- **Never cache auth-sensitive data** — user-specific results in shared cache keys cause data leaks

Django's caching framework has three levels: full-page caching with `@cache_page`, template fragment caching with `{% cache %}`, and low-level cache API with `cache.get/set`. For a high-traffic API, I'd use Redis as the backend (via `django-redis`) with explicit per-object caching at the service layer.

The strategy I follow: cache expensive DB queries and computed results, not raw model instances (which can go stale). Use meaningful cache keys that include version identifiers. Set explicit TTLs — never set `None` (infinite) in production. Invalidate on write using signals or explicit cache.delete calls in the service layer.

For stampede prevention when a cache key expires and many requests hit the DB simultaneously: use dog-pile prevention with a short lock, or pre-warm the cache before expiry with a Celery task.

- **`IGNORE_EXCEPTIONS: True`** — production must degrade gracefully if Redis is unavailable
- **Version your cache keys** — incrementing `CACHE_VERSION` invalidates all keys without flushing Redis
- **Never cache auth-sensitive data** — user-specific data must never bleed into shared cache keys
- **Use `cache.get_many()` and `cache.set_many()`** — batch operations reduce round trips

questions.title: Celery Async Tasks in Django
questions.question: How do you implement asynchronous task processing in Django with Celery, and what are common pitfalls?

sections.content: They want to see you can configure Celery + Redis/RabbitMQ, write idempotent tasks, handle retries with backoff, and understand the common failure patterns: task leakage, database connection exhaustion, non-idempotent tasks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pass IDs, not model instances** — objects serialized at enqueue time are stale when the worker executes
- **Idempotent tasks are mandatory** — retries happen on crashes and timeouts; check state before acting
- **Set hard and soft time limits** — `TASK_TIME_LIMIT` kills zombie workers; `SOFT_TIME_LIMIT` lets tasks clean up
- **Exponential backoff with jitter** — `retry_backoff=True` and `retry_jitter=True` prevent thundering herd on retries
- **Separate queues for priority** — `@shared_task(queue='emails')` prevents slow bulk jobs from blocking critical tasks

Celery turns Python functions into distributed tasks. Django views enqueue work; Celery workers running separately execute it asynchronously. The message broker (Redis or RabbitMQ) sits in between.

The setup is: configure Celery in `celery.py`, mark functions with `@shared_task`, and call them with `.delay()` or `.apply_async()`. The key discipline is making tasks idempotent — if the same task runs twice (worker crash mid-execution, retry after timeout), the result should be the same. Also: tasks should be small and focused. Never pass Django model instances as arguments — they go stale. Pass IDs and re-query inside the task.

Common pitfalls: tasks that hold database transactions open (use `@transaction.atomic` inside the task, not before `.delay()`), tasks that silently fail with no retry policy, and tasks that fan out into thousands of sub-tasks without rate limiting.

- **Pass IDs, not objects** — model instances serialized at enqueue time are stale when the task runs
- **Make tasks idempotent** — retries happen; check before acting, use atomic updates
- **Set time limits** — `CELERY_TASK_TIME_LIMIT` prevents zombie workers
- **Use separate queues** — `@shared_task(queue='emails')` for priority separation
- **Monitor with Flower** or Prometheus — dead workers and queue depth are critical alerts
- **Beat scheduler** for cron-like periodic tasks — never `crontab` + management commands in production

questions.title: DRF Authentication
questions.question: How does authentication work in Django REST Framework, and how would you implement JWT auth?

sections.content: They want to see you understand DRF's authentication class system, can implement JWT, and know the difference between authentication (who you are) and permission (what you can do).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authentication ≠ Permissions** — DRF separates who you are (auth classes) from what you can do (permission classes)
- **Return `None`, don't raise** — when the auth scheme doesn't match, returning `None` lets other auth classes try
- **Short-lived access + long-lived refresh** — 15-minute access tokens with 7-day refresh tokens balance security and UX
- **Blacklist enables true logout** — server-side refresh token storage lets you revoke sessions immediately
- **JWT is encoded, not encrypted** — never put sensitive data in the payload; anyone with the token can decode it

DRF separates authentication (identifying the caller) from permissions (deciding what they can do). Authentication classes attempt to identify the user from the request — if successful, `request.user` and `request.auth` are set. If no class succeeds, the view gets an anonymous user.

For JWT: on login, sign a payload (user_id, exp) with your secret key and return it. On subsequent requests, the client sends it in the Authorization header as `Bearer <token>`. A custom authentication class decodes and validates the token, fetches the user, and sets `request.user`.

I'd use `djangorestframework-simplejwt` in most projects — it handles token rotation, refresh tokens, and blacklisting out of the box. Custom implementation makes sense when you need claims from an external identity provider or custom token structure.

- **Return `None` (not raise) when scheme doesn't match** — allows other auth classes to try
- **Short-lived access tokens + longer refresh tokens** — 15min access, 7-day refresh is a common pattern
- **Store refresh tokens server-side** (blacklist) — enables true logout
- **Never put sensitive data in JWT payload** — it's base64-encoded, not encrypted
- **Use HTTPS only** — JWTs in Authorization headers are plaintext to anyone with network access

questions.title: QuerySet Optimization
questions.question: What are the most important Django QuerySet optimization techniques for a high-traffic application?

sections.content: A senior-level question. They want concrete techniques with code, not just buzzwords. Explain N+1, bulk operations, indexing, and query analysis.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fix N+1 first** — `select_related` for ForeignKey/OneToOne, `prefetch_related` for ManyToMany/reverse FK
- **`values()` and `only()` cut memory** — fetch only needed columns; `values()` skips model instantiation entirely
- **Bulk operations over loops** — `bulk_create` fires one query instead of 10,000 individual INSERTs
- **Composite indexes on filter columns** — `Meta.indexes` speeds up queries that filter on multiple fields together
- **`F()` expressions prevent race conditions** — arithmetic in SQL avoids read-modify-write bugs in concurrent updates

The biggest wins in Django query optimization come from five areas: fixing N+1 queries with `select_related`/`prefetch_related`, reducing data fetched with `only()`/`values()`, using `bulk_create`/`bulk_update` instead of loops, adding database indexes via `Meta.indexes`, and analyzing slow queries with `connection.queries` or EXPLAIN.

N+1 is the most impactful fix — going from 1+N queries to 1 or 2 queries is often a 100x improvement. After that, `values()` instead of full model instances for read-only endpoints can halve memory usage. Bulk operations matter when importing data or doing batch updates — a loop calling `save()` 10,000 times fires 10,000 queries; `bulk_create` fires one.

- **Use `iterator()`** for large querysets — avoids loading all rows into memory
- **`F()` expressions** do math in SQL, not Python — no read-modify-write race conditions
- **`exists()` over `count() > 0`** — `SELECT 1` is faster than `SELECT COUNT(*)`
- **`get_or_create()` is not atomic** — use with `transaction.atomic()` to prevent race conditions
- **Profile in production-like load** — a query fast on 100 rows may be slow on 10 million
